Yes—under those conditions, you should have a good chance of spotting the Moon.

- It is **18.2° above the horizon**, toward **azimuth 201°**—roughly **south-southwest**.
- It is a thin **11.4% crescent**, so it will be much less conspicuous than a half or full Moon.
- Its **39° separation from the Sun** is favorable: far enough from the Sun to be reasonably safe and visible, while still placing it in the daytime sky.
- At about **376,000 km**, its distance is normal and not a meaningful obstacle.
- Clear skies and ordinary unaided eyesight should be sufficient, though daylight glare and the thin crescent make it challenging.

Look about **18° above the south-southwestern horizon**—roughly two fist-widths above the horizon at arm’s length. First use the Sun’s position only as a reference, but **do not look directly at it**. Binoculars can help you locate the Moon, but use them only after positioning yourself so the Sun is safely out of the binoculars’ field of view; once found, you should be able to see it unaided.

The Moon may appear as a small, faint crescent against the blue sky rather than an obvious bright disk.
